           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                      )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                        ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                      )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                       )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                          )
          PURSUANT 17 O.S. § 286(C)                                )

         HEARING:              September 8–9, 2026, in Concourse Theater, C50 (live and virtual
                                      teleconference)
                               Will Rogers Memorial Office Building

                               Before Shawnae Robey, Administrative Law Judge

         APPEARANCES:          A. Chase Snodgrass and Deborah R. Thompson, Attorneys representing

                PROPOSED JOINT FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

                This Case comes before the Corporation Commission (“Commission”) of the State of
         Oklahoma, being regularly in session and the Commissioners present and participating, for
         consideration and action on the Application of Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or
         “Company”) filed on May 1, 2026, requesting approval of three Electric Service Agreements
         (“ESAs”) with Alliance Site & Grid, LLC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Google, LLC (“Google”),
         and preapproval of two Capacity Purchase Agreements (“CPAs”) pursuant to 17 O.S. § 286(C),
         and authorization to recover CPA costs through OG&E’s Fuel Adjustment Clause (“FCA”).
                 Following the filing of Direct, Responsive, and Rebuttal Testimony, OG&E, the Public
         Utility Division of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“PUD”), the Office of the Oklahoma
         Attorney General (“Attorney General”), and Google submitted a Joint Stipulation and Settlement
         Agreement (“Joint Stipulation”), including Exhibit A, Customer Impact Review Protocol,
         resolving the issues in this proceeding. Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”) did not
         join the Joint Stipulation but stated that it did not intend to present testimony in opposition.
         Oklahoma Sustainability Network (“OSN”) was excused from the hearing and did not participate.


         Case No. PUD2026-000031                                                                       1
         Proposed Joint Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law

         (9/9/26 Tr. 7:18–25; 8:1–14; 9:10–16; 9:18–25; 10:1–20.) The Joint Stipulation and Settlement
         Agreement is attached hereto as Attachment “A” and is incorporated as if set forth fully herein.
                                          I. PROCEDURAL HISTORY

                    [PLACEHOLDER - PROCEDURAL HISTORY TO BE INSERTED]



                A Pre-Hearing Conference was held and Public Comment was taken on September 8, 2026.
         The Hearing on the Merits was held before Administrative Law Judge Shawnae Robey on
         September 9, 2026. At the Hearing on the Merits, the parties presented the Joint Stipulation and
         Settlement Agreement and testimony in support thereof. (9/9/26 Tr. 12–55.)
                                                   II. NOTICE
                At the Pre-Hearing Conference, counsel for OG&E announced that notice to the public had
         been provided in compliance with Order No. 758316 and the associated Customer Notice
         Affidavit, which includes a copy of the Notice provided to customers, was filed of record on
         September 3, 2026. The ALJ finds that notice has been accomplished in compliance with Order
         No. 758316 and Commission rules.
                                          III. SUMMARY OF EVIDENCE
                 Documents filed in this Case, including pre-filed Direct, Responsive and Rebuttal
         Testimony, are contained in the records maintained by the Court Clerk of the Commission. In
         addition to the pre-filed testimony, parties presented live testimony at the Hearing on the Merits
         in support of the Joint Stipulation. Including herein is Attachment “B” which provides a summary
         of the pre-filed testimony and a summary of the relevant live testimony provided at the Hearing is
         set forth below, which is reflected in full of the transcript of the proceedings. The Commission
         has reviewed the evidentiary record, the Joint Stipulation, and the related testimony in reaching
         the findings and conclusions set forth below.
         A. Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company Pre-Filed Direct and Rebuttal Testimony
                 OG&E witness Kimber L. Shoop testified regarding OG&E’s capacity need, the statutory
         requirements of 17 O.S. § 286(C), and the reasonableness of the CPAs in light of available
         alternatives. He further testified that the ESAs contain substantial protections designed to ensure
         that costs attributable to serving Google are not shifted to other customer classes and that any
         future adverse rate impact may be reviewed and addressed by the Commission. In rebuttal he
         addresses Section 286(C) and discusses the “fail safe” provision. (Shoop Direct 3:7–10; 4:1–29;
         5:1–3; 5:12–26; 6:1–5; 7:Chart 1 and 2, 1–5; 11:15–28; 9:20–27; 10:4–13 and 17–21; Shoop
         Rebuttal 3:9–30; 4:1–2; 5:24–29; 6:1–8; 6:12–28.)
                OG&E witness John P. Laws described the overall business arrangement with Google for
         three new Oklahoma data centers and the principal protections contained in the ESAs. He
         explained that Google will fund 100 percent of the dedicated transmission infrastructure necessary
         to connect each site through contributions in aid of construction, while OG&E will acquire a
         portion of the capacity needed to meet its identified resource adequacy requirements through the
         two CPAs. He also describes the Supplemental Resource Administrative Charge (“SRAC”)

         Proposed Joint Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law

         charge, along with the long-term service commitments, minimum billing obligations, exit and
         capacity-reduction fees, credit support, and other contractual provisions intended to protect
         existing customers. (Laws Direct 3:22–30; 4:1–2; 4:26–31; 5:1; 7:23–26; 8:13–17, 20–31; 9:2–5;
         9:8–11; 9:24–30.)
                 OG&E witness Gwin Cash explained the rate design, cost allocation, minimum billing
         demand and energy provisions, and other customer protections contained in the ESAs. He testified
         that the agreements preserve the ability for Google’s rates to migrate to a future Commission-
         approved large-load tariff if applicable, while the non-rate contractual protections remain in effect
         according to the agreements through the term of the ESAs. (Cash Direct 3:13–19; 4:10–30; 5:26–
         31.)
                 OG&E witness Matthew J. Schuermann supported preapproval of the Rush Springs and
         High Spring CPAs. He testified that the two 15-year CPAs provide approximately 360 MW of
         accredited summer capacity and 120 MW of accredited winter capacity and are priced below the
         capacity alternatives available to OG&E through its 2024 All-Source Request for Proposals. He
         further testified that the agreements contain delivery and replacement protections and provide
         needed capacity without transferring energy-market price risk to OG&E customers. In Rebuttal
         Testimony, Mr. Schuermann supported the favorable evaluation of the CPAs compared to
         reasonable alternatives available to OG&E. (Schuermann Direct 3:30–31; 4:1–7; 4:9–14; 5:5–16;
         5:22–31; Schuermann Rebuttal 3:5–19; 5:19–21; 6:3–13.)
                 OG&E witness Jason J. Thenmadathil presented analyses of the effect of Google’s load on
         existing customer classes and explained the customer-impact review contemplated by the ESAs.
         He testified that Google’s large and relatively steady load contributes to shared system costs and
         can place downward pressure on rates for existing customers. His rebuttal testimony also
         addressed the appropriate treatment of future costs and the importance of using actual, customer-
         specific information when future customer-impact reviews are conducted. (Thenmadathil Direct
         4:1–15; 5:1–16; Thenmadathil Rebuttal 3:21–29; 4:1–6.)
                 OG&E witness Matthew DeCourcey addressed industry practice concerning service to
         very large loads. He testified that the ESAs contain protections against stranded costs and cross-
         subsidization that are consistent with, and in several respects stronger than, protections observed
         in other jurisdictions. He further explained that the unique contractual fail-safe mechanism permits
         future review and correction if circumstances change. (DeCourcey Direct 4:12–28; 5:1–6; 10:1–
         12; 13:1–9; 15:12–14; 17:17–20; 18:5–12; 20:12–25; 21:1–2; 21:4–8.)
         B. Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers Pre-Filed Responsive Testimony
                 In response to the testimony of OG&E, OIEC witness Mark E. Garrett concluded that the
         cost-of-service analyses presented in this Case were reasonable and appropriate to show that
         Google’s load provides a net benefit to OG&E’s system at this time. He also concluded that the
         consumer protections in the ESAs demonstrate a fair and reasonable approach consistent with his
         recommendation in the PSO proceeding (Case No. PUD2025-000075) and are sufficient to protect
         other OG&E customers. He recommended continued review in future rate cases to demonstrate
         there is no net detriment to the system. (Garrett Responsive 6:1–10; 11:7–9; 15:20–21; 17:4–6;
         17:10–11.)
         C. Office of the Oklahoma Attorney General Pre-Filed Responsive Testimony



         Case No. PUD2026-000031                                                                            3

                 Attorney General witness Frank J. Beling evaluated the CPAs, the ESAs, and additional
         consumer protections. He testified that OG&E has a need for the capacity reflected in the CPAs
         and the CPAs have favorable pricing compared with the other capacity options available through
         OG&E’s 2024 RFP and, based on the particular facts and circumstances of this Case, the Attorney
         General did not object to their selection. He further testified that the proposed special contracts
         comply with House Bill 2992 and that the Attorney General did not object to approval of the ESAs,
         including the SRAC which is acceptable because it is between Google and OG&E and does not
         affect other customers’ rates. He recommended that while the “failsafe” analysis is a beneficial
         mechanism to identify any adverse rate impacts, he argued the analysis needed more details on the
         methodology. He further supported that should there be future network transmission upgrades
         required to serve Google’s load, Google should pre-fund those costs and that large-load customers
         should pay their fair share of any approved Construction Work In Progress (“CWIP”). (Beling
         Responsive 6:17–20; 7:1-–2; 8:1–15; 8:17–19; 14:19–20; 15:1–2; 16:5–8; 24:11–18; 27:1–13;
         28:5–17; 29:10–15; 32:13–15; 32:18–19; 33:12–14.)
         D. Public Utility Division Pre-Filed Responsive Testimony
                 PUD witness John Givens addressed the proposed ESAs and CPAs, customer protections,
         potential impacts of the Google load on existing customers, and the appropriate framework for
         future customer-impact reviews. Mr. Givens concluded that the ESAs contain reasonable
         protections for existing customers, meet the requirements of HB 2992, and recognized the
         importance of reviewing future rate impacts as actual costs and loads become known. He
         recommended periodic review of the cost-of-service impacts associated with Google’s load and
         proposed mechanisms for addressing any adverse impacts identified in future proceedings. Mr.
         Givens also addressed OG&E’s consideration of reasonable alternatives to the CPAs and the
         standards that should apply when generation resources are acquired outside a competitive
         solicitation. (Givens Responsive 3:16–19; 3:24–25; 4:9–15; 9:6–15; 13:17–19; 14:1–7; 15:11–14;
         16:11–19; 17:8; 21:7–9; 21;14–15; 22:3–5.)
                 PUD witness Frank Mossburg evaluated OG&E’s need for additional generation capacity,
         the proposed CPAs, the protections contained in the ESAs, and the methodology for evaluating
         the future customer impacts of Google’s load. Mr. Mossburg concluded that OG&E demonstrated
         a need for new generation supply; that the CPAs contain standard contractual protections, are
         priced below recent market transactions, and represent a unique opportunity; and that the ESAs
         contain reasonable protections for ratepayers. He further recommended that the Commission
         establish guidelines for evaluating the impact of the new load in future proceedings so that actual
         rate setting appropriately protects existing customers from adverse cost shifts. (Mossburg
         Responsive 24:4–12.)
         E. Google LLC Pre-Filed Rebuttal Testimony
                  In his Rebuttal Testimony, Google witness Adrian J. Kimbrough supported approval of the
         ESAs and addressed the appropriate framework for future customer-impact assessments. He
         testified that Google is prepared to pay the incremental costs directly caused by serving its load,
         and future assessments should distinguish Google-caused costs from system costs. His testimony
         supported considering methodologies to review the cost shifts in future proceedings. (Kimbrough
         Rebuttal 4:5–8; 5:3–5; 11:5–19; 15:5–9 15:14–16.)




         Case No. PUD2026-000031                                                                          4
         Proposed Joint Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law

         F. Joint Stipulation and Settlement Agreement
                 At the Hearing on the Merits the Commission heard testimony regarding the Joint
         Stipulation. The Joint Stipulation recommends (1) approval of the three ESAs, preapproval of the
         Rush Springs and High Spring CPAs pursuant to 17 O.S. § 286(C), recovery of CPA costs through
         the FCA subject to annual prudence review, (2) details of a Customer Impact Assessment, (3)
         addresses transmission costs, (4) Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”), (5) certain annual
         projections, (6) approval of the Supplemental Resource Administrative Charge (“SRAC”) as
         proposed in the Application, and (7) requires certain forecasts during the Integrated Resource
         Planning (“IRP”) process. In particular, the Joint Stipulation establishes a Customer Impact
         Assessment framework, with Exhibit A providing a Customer Impact Review Protocol intended
         as a starting framework for future assessments, while preserving the Commission’s authority and
         the parties’ ability to address the methodology in future proceedings. (9/9/26 Tr. 23:14–25; 24:1–
         25; 25:1–19; 26:3–14.)
                 OG&E witness Kimber Shoop testified in support of the Joint Stipulation. Mr. Shoop
         described the settlement negotiations as robust and testified that the Joint Stipulation constitutes a
         fair, just, and reasonable compromise of the issues in the case. Mr. Shoop summarized the
         principal provisions of the Joint Stipulation, including Part II Paragraph A’s approval of the three
         ESAs as special contracts and grant Section 286(C) preapproval of the two CPAs with FCA
         recovery subject to annual prudence review. (9/9/26 Tr. 22:22–25; 23:1–3; 23:20–25; 24:1–3.)
                 Mr. Shoop explained that the ESAs were negotiated to permit OG&E to serve Google’s
         substantial new load while protecting existing customers from adverse rate impacts. He identified
         protections including substantial Contribution In Aid of Constriction (“CIAC”) payments,
         significant performance security, a long-term service commitment, exit fees, minimum demand
         and energy payments, and allocation of costs based on contract demand. (9/9/26 Tr. 13:7–25;
         14:1–3; 15:1–5; 17:1–25; 18:1–25; 19:1–11.)
                 Mr. Shoop further testified that the Rush Springs and High Spring CPAs will help meet
         OG&E’s capacity obligations, were negotiated at prices below those reflected in OG&E’s recent
         RFP, will benefit all customers rather than being dedicated solely to Google, and are proposed for
         recovery through the Fuel Adjustment Clause. He further stated ESAs will be governed during
         their term by the terms and conditions of service. He described that Paragraph A also requests
         approval of the SRAC paid to OG&E for administering the CPAs. (9/9/26 Tr. 19:19–25; 20:1–16;
         21:5–13; 24:3–6.)
                 He then addressed Paragraph B regarding the Customer Impact Assessment and described
         how OG&E agreed it would conduct the with-and-without Google analysis in order to ensure
         customers would not be harmed by the addition of the Google load. He described how the
         Customer Impact Review Protocol in Exhibit A to the Joint Stipulation was adopted as starting
         principles for future with-and-without-Google analyses in future rate cases. He explained that the
         framework is not intended to bind the Commission or the parties to a single methodology in future
         proceedings and that the Commission will remain the ultimate arbiter of the appropriate
         methodology. (9/9/26 Tr. 23:11–15; 24:16–24; 25:1–25; 26:1–25; 27:1–3.)
                 As to Paragraph C, Mr. Shoop testified that Google has already agreed to fund 100 percent
         (and has already paid) for the dedicated transmission and distribution infrastructure needed to serve
         their load through CIAC. However, parties wanted to ensure that should any future transmission

         costs come up in the future as a direct result of the Google load, that would be addressed as
         described in Paragraph C. (9/9/26 Tr. (9/9/26 Tr. 26:7–12; 27:13–25; 28:1–19.)
                As to Paragraph D, Mr. Shoop described how this paragraph ensures that any concerns
         raised in testimony regarding recovery of Construction Work In Progress (“CWIP”) from
         customers would also be collected from Google. (9/9/26 Tr. 28:22–25; 29:1–3.)
                  As to Paragraph E, Mr. Shoop described how in this provision OG&E agreed to provide to
         the Attorney General and PUD a 12-month projection of minimum bill revenues per site within 90
         days of a final order and the updated annually until full contract demand is reached and, because
         it is customer-specific information, it would be provided to the Attorney General and PUD on a
         highly sensitive, confidential basis. He further described that this provision agrees that any cost
         components that are moved into rate base become subject to billing minimums established in the
         ESAs. In addition, Paragraph E requires OG&E to track the revenues it receives from Google for
         the SRAC. (9/9/26 Tr. 29:12–25; 30:4–19.)
                As to Paragraph F regarding resource adequacy tracking, OG&E has agreed to provide
         forecast information for the large load customer class on a highly sensitive, confidential basis in a
         manner that will not identify any customer-specific information. (9/9/26 Tr. 30:11–19.)
                 Mr. Shoop ultimately recommended that the Commission approve the Joint Stipulation,
         including approval of the ESAs and CPAs, and find the settlement fair, just, reasonable, and in the
         public interest. (9/9/26 Tr. 32:6–16.)
                 Attorney General witness Frank Beling testified in support of approval of the Joint
         Stipulation. He agreed with Mr. Shoop’s description of the settlement terms and did not identify
         any additional terms requiring clarification. Mr. Beling emphasized the importance of Exhibit A
         to the Joint Stipulation, explaining that the Customer Impact Review Protocol provides needed
         detail concerning how future customer impacts may be evaluated and serves as a useful roadmap
         while preserving the parties’ ability to address the methodology in future proceedings. Mr. Beling
         also agreed with Mr. Shoop’s characterization of the settlement and testified that Exhibit A
         provides helpful detail for future calculations and constitutes an important safeguard for other
         customers. Mr. Beling further testified that the Joint Stipulation addresses the Attorney General’s
         concerns, reflects a collaborative compromise, and believes it is fair, just, reasonable, and in the
         public interest. He recommended that the Commission approve the Joint Stipulation. (9/9/26 Tr.
         46:14–24; 47:1–25; 48:1–18; 49:3–15.)
                  PUD witness David Scalf testified on behalf of PUD and explained that, due to staff
         departures, he had assumed responsibility for the matter, had reviewed the testimony, discovery,
         and responses in the Case, and had participated in all settlement negotiations. He testified in
         support of the Joint Stipulation. Mr. Scalf characterized the settlement negotiations as involving
         substantial give-and-take and robust discussion. He testified that Exhibit A to the Joint Stipulation
         was a significant subject of negotiation and underwent multiple revisions before agreement was
         reached. Mr. Scalf agreed with the settlement testimony provided by Mr. Shoop and Mr. Beling,
         testified that the Joint Stipulation is fair, just, and reasonable and is in the public interest, and
         recommended that the Commission adopt and approve the Joint Stipulation. (9/9/26 Tr. 52:1–19;
         52:20–24; 53:5–7; 53:8–25; 54:3–19.)
                Following review of the record in this Case, the Joint Stipulation, and the testimony
         provided in support of the Joint Stipulation, the Administrative Law Judge recommended that

         OG&E’s Application be approved as modified by the Joint Stipulation and Settlement Agreement,
         and recommended approval of the Joint Stipulation and Settlement Agreement. (9/9/26 Tr. 57:1–
         7.)
                          IV. FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
                THE COMMISSION FINDS that it has jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties
         pursuant to Article IX, § 18 of the Oklahoma Constitution, 17 O.S. §§ 152, 153, and 286(C), the
         Commission’s Rules of Practice, OAC 165:5, and the Commission’s Electric Utility Rules, OAC
         165:35.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that notice in this Case was proper, provided as
         required by law, Commission rules, and Order No. 758316.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that the Joint Stipulation resolves all disputed
         issues in this Case and is supported by the evidentiary record; is fair, just, and reasonable, and in
         the public interest; and should be approved in its entirety.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that OG&E’s Application, as modified by the
         Joint Stipulation, should be approved.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that OG&E executed three ESAs for retail
         electric service to three new Oklahoma data center sites. The ESAs contain long-term service
         commitments, minimum billing demand and energy provisions, credit support, termination and
         capacity-reduction protections, requirements for customer funding of dedicated transmission and
         distribution infrastructure, and provisions allowing future Commission review of potential adverse
         rate impacts.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that the ESAs contain reasonable and substantial
         customer protections designed to mitigate stranded-cost risk, cost shifting, and other financial risks
         to existing OG&E customers and comply with the customer-protection requirements of House Bill
         2992 (2026), codified at 17 O.S. §§ 900–906.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that the three ESAs should be approved as special
         contracts under OAC 165:35-1-2 and deemed tariffs under OAC 165:35-5-1(d)
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that OG&E has demonstrated a need for
         generation capacity provided for by the two CPAs within the meaning of 17 O.S. § 286(C).
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that OG&E considered reasonable alternatives
         as set forth in 17 O.S. § 286(C) to the Rush Springs and High Spring CPAs and the record
         demonstrates that the CPAs were compared against capacity alternatives available through
         OG&E’s 2024 All-Source RFP and market alternatives and provide favorable pricing relative to
         those alternatives.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that the Rush Springs and High Spring CPAs are
         reasonable, prudent, and in the public interest and should be preapproved pursuant to 17 O.S. §
         286(C).
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that, pursuant to 17 O.S. § 286(C), the Rush
         Springs and High Spring CPAs are considered used and useful, and recovery of the associated
         capacity costs through OG&E’s FCA, subject to annual prudence review, is reasonable and should
         be approved.

         Case No. PUD2026-000031                                                                             7
         Proposed Joint Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 152 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/16/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 9




                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that the Customer Impact Review Protocol
         attached to the Joint Stipulation as Exhibit A provides a reasonable starting framework for future
         Customer Impact Assessments, while preserving the ability of the Commission and the parties to
         consider refinements or alternative methodologies in future proceedings based on the facts and
         evidence then available.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that Google is required to fund 100 percent of
         dedicated transmission and distribution infrastructure as CIAC.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that OG&E, consistent with cost causation
         principles as required by 17 O.S. Section 900–906, has not identified any necessary regional or
         network upgrades as a direct result of the Google load.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that should the Southwest Power Pool identify
         any regional or network upgrades as a result of the Google load, OG&E and Google will negotiate
         regarding such costs and OG&E will propose a methodology to the Commission in a future
         proceeding, all as set forth in the Joint Stipulation.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that, as specified in the Joint Stipulation, if CWIP
         is approved by the Commission to be recovered from customers, CWIP shall also be collected
         from Google.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that it is reasonable and appropriate for OG&E
         to provide as Highly Sensitive Confidential to the Attorney General and the Public Utility Division
         a 12-month projection of minimum bill revenues per site until each site reaches full Contract
         Demand as set forth in the Joint Stipulation.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that the SRAC as proposed by OG&E is
         reasonable and should be approved subject to the requirement that OG&E separately track these
         revenues as set forth in the Joint Stipulation.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER FINDS that during the Integrated Resource Planning
         process OG&E agrees to provide as Highly Confidential and subject to a protective order the
         forecast attributable to the XLPL Tariff customer class without any customer identifiable
         information as set forth in the Joint Stipulation.


                                                   ORDER
                THE COMMISSION ORDERS that the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law set forth
         above are adopted as the Order of the Commission.
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER ORDERS that OG&E’s Application, as modified by the
         Joint Stipulation and Settlement Agreement, is hereby approved.
               THE COMMISSION FURTHER ORDERS that the Joint Stipulation and Settlement
         Agreement, including Exhibit A, Customer Impact Review Protocol, as attached hereto as
         Attachment “A” is hereby approved and adopted.
                THE COMMISSION FURTHER ORDERS that the three Electric Service Agreements
         between Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company and Alliance Site & Grid, LLC, a wholly-owned
         subsidiary of Google, LLC are approved.

                THE COMMISSION FURTHER ORDERS that the Rush Springs and High Spring
         Capacity Purchase Agreements are preapproved pursuant to 17 O.S. § 286(C).
                 THE COMMISSION FURTHER ORDERS that OG&E is authorized to recover the costs
         of the Rush Springs and High Spring CPAs through its Fuel Adjustment Clause, subject to annual
         prudence review.
               THE COMMISSION FURTHER                 ORDERS      that   the   Supplemental   Resource
         Administrative Charge is approved.
